title: Movements for rights since 1945
log: 2026-11-12T12:44:19Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The new point covers five movements (civil rights, Indigenous rights, women's rights, LGBTQI+ rights and environmental movements), but the closest bank points each cover only one movement at a different depth, so none teaches the same idea.

draft.title: Movements for rights since 1945
card: After 1945, groups of people organised movements to win rights or protect things they valued. They included civil rights, Indigenous rights, women's rights, LGBTQI+ rights and environmental movements.
Protest
Marches, strikes, sit-ins and petitions. They draw public attention and put pressure on governments.
Courts
Legal cases that challenge unfair laws or test whether a right is protected.
Elections
Voting, and campaigning for candidates and parties, so that governments pass new laws or change old ones.
draft.remember: Rights movements used protest, courts and elections to change laws and attitudes.

a.q: A group holds marches and sit-ins to demand an end to a law it sees as unfair. Which method is the group using?
opts: Protest, to draw attention and pressure the government
Courts, to test the law through a legal case
Elections, to vote the government out of office
Petitions only, which are not a form of protest
a.why: Marches and sit-ins are protest. They make a problem public and pressure leaders to act. Courts are different: they involve legal cases, not public demonstrations.
a.clue: Think about actions in streets and public places.

b.q: A group of citizens in Perth wants a new law to protect a local river. They argue that the existing law does not protect it, and a judge examines that claim. Which method are they using?
opts: Courts, as a legal case tests what the law protects
Protest, as a judge only hears public marches
Elections, as a judge decides who governs
Attitudes, as courts change opinions but not laws
b.why: A judge examining whether a law protects the river means the group has taken a legal case, so it is using the courts. Protest is tempting because the group wants change, but no march or demonstration is described.
b.clue: Who is examining the claim, and where?

a.best: Protest, to draw attention and pressure the government

b.best: Courts, as a legal case tests what the law protects

problems.detail: The stem says the group 'wants a new law', but a court case cannot make a new law. Seeking a new law fits elections or lobbying better. The case is really testing whether the existing law protects the river, so the scenario muddles the methods it is meant to separate.
The wrong options are implausible ('a judge decides who governs', 'a judge only hears public marches', 'Attitudes' is not a method). A student can pick Courts without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The card and question a are accurate. Question b's scenario mixes up methods: wanting a 'new law' fits elections or lobbying, while the court tests the existing law. Its wrong options are also too implausible to test understanding.

proposal.title: Movements for rights since 1945
card: After 1945, groups of people organised movements to win rights or protect things they valued, and to change laws and attitudes. They included civil rights, Indigenous rights, women's rights, LGBTQI+ rights and environmental movements.
Protest
Marches, strikes, sit-ins and petitions. They draw public attention and put pressure on governments.
Courts
Legal cases that challenge unfair laws or test whether a right is protected. A judge decides what the law means.
Elections
Voting, and campaigning for candidates and parties, so that governments pass new laws or change old ones.
proposal.remember: Rights movements used protest, courts and elections to change laws and attitudes.

a.q: A group holds marches and sit-ins to demand an end to a law it sees as unfair. Which method is the group using?
opts: Protest, to draw attention and pressure the government
Courts, to test the law through a legal case
Elections, to vote the government out of office
Protest, which asks a judge to cancel the law
a.why: Marches and sit-ins are protest. They make a problem public and pressure leaders to act. Protest does not ask a judge to rule on a law: that happens through a legal case in the courts.
a.clue: Think about actions in streets and public places.

b.q: A group in Perth believes a mining company's plan breaks an existing law that protects a local river. It asks a judge to stop the plan, and the case is widely reported. Which method is the group using?
opts: Courts, using a legal case to test what the law protects
Protest, using public pressure to make the government act
Elections, backing candidates who will pass a new law
Petitions, collecting signatures to show public support
b.why: The group asks a judge to decide whether the existing law protects the river, so it is using the courts. Protest is tempting because the case gets public attention, but no march, strike or petition is described.
